title: Solid Workshop
context: Grade 4, and the chapter's only work in three dimensions. An adult sees shapes being counted and folded. What is actually being settled is what a face, an edge and a vertex are, well enough to count them on a solid the chapter's table leaves out, which is what the page's find-out task asks for. The printed pages need care in three places: they say a pyramid's faces are all triangular beside a square pyramid with a square base, they call a square prism also known as a cube without saying its height must match its base, and they draw a box's side view taller than its front view.

writeup.why: Count what a solid is made of, sort it by its bases, fold one up from flat, and look at it from three sides.
writeup.look: A solid on a turntable with three counters at the top left of the canvas, a net bench below it, and a view window with three small cameras at the right.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Solid Workshop' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the faces, the edges and the vertices, the corners, counted so far, three numbers in ink under their own headings and always in that order, each climbing by one as its part is lit. On the third phase it carries the creases folded against the creases the net has, and on the fourth the views drawn against the three cameras. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The turntable stands at the left of the working area, 360 by 470 at 64,214, with one solid drawn on it in a simple three-quarter view, its visible edges deep blue and its hidden edges grey and dashed, turning a quarter turn at a time to show every side. Tapping a face lights it green and adds one to the face count; tracing along a line where two faces meet lights that edge amber and adds one to the edge count; tapping a corner drops a vermilion dot on it as a vertex and adds one to the vertex count. A part already counted stays lit and cannot be counted twice, a curved face lights with a curved sheen, and a cone's tip takes a dot as its one vertex, though no two edges meet there. The bench fills the middle, 420 by 470 at 440,214. On the second phase it is the sorting bench, with the headings prism and pyramid across its top: the base light lights a solid's base, or both its bases, green, and the solid is set under the heading its bases and other faces call for, the base itself keeping whatever shape it has. On the third it is the net bench, holding in one flat piece a net of up to six squares, each 66 on a side, or of rectangles and triangles; the fold control raises the faces along their creases one at a time, and a net that closes meets every edge, while one that cannot close shows two faces landing on one place, glowing sky blue, and a side left open. The view window stands at the right, 274 by 470 at 876,214: the top view in its upper part, 274 by 170 at 876,226, and the front and side views side by side beneath it, each 130 by 170, at 876,420 and 1014,420, all drawn at one scale with near-black guide lines running level from the top of one view to the top of the next. The size strip runs under them, 274 by 50 at 876,610, holding the measurements every view of the solid shares. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a count or a measurement is asked for, and a word pad wherever a solid, a face or a view is named, with keys reading cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere, prism, pyramid, square, rectangle, triangle and circle. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The figure being studied, every line, segment, ray, side, outline, circle, angle arm and visible edge of a solid, is deep blue. Every point, end point, corner dot, vertex dot and the centre dot of a circle is vermilion. A length being measured, walked, added or named, and every angle arc and square corner mark, is amber. The unit squares that cover an area, the flood inside a closed figure and a face of a solid being counted are green. A line of symmetry or a mirror line is reddish purple and always dotted. The second thing set beside the first, a fold being tried, a mirror image, the other half of a fold, a chord that is not a diameter and the larger angle between clock hands, is sky blue. A hidden edge of a solid is grey and dashed, and grey is used for nothing else. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every grid line, ruler tick, bracket, guide line and table rule is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a point is a round dot, a line carries an arrowhead at each end, a ray a dot and one arrowhead and a segment a dot at each end, a measured length carries its number, a hidden edge is dashed and a line of symmetry is dotted, before any of them is told by a colour. A dotted line always means a true line of symmetry or a mirror line, and a fold being tried is drawn solid until it is kept, so nothing else on any stage of this chapter is ever dotted. Hidden edges are the only dashed lines on this stage, and every vertex counted is a round vermilion dot. The three counts never share a box and always stand in one order, faces, edges, vertices, so a number is read by its heading and never by where it happens to sit.
writeup.finish: The card shows the solid the child counted with its three counts, the net they folded standing closed beside it, and its three views at one scale.

phases.win: the counts stop at six, twelve and eight, with every part of the box lit
phases.does: spins the solid, taps every face, traces every edge and dots every corner
phases.goal: a face is a surface, an edge is where two faces meet, and a vertex is a corner, each counted on its own
phases.says: Spin it round. Count the faces first, then the edges, then the corners.
phases.check: Away from the screen: count the faces, edges and vertices of a closed box, with a sticker on each part as you count it.
phases.feels: faces, edges and corners are three different counts, and each one is kept in its own place
phases.hands: Hand each group a closed cardboard box. Touch and count its faces, then run a finger along each edge where two faces meet, then touch each corner, which is called a vertex. Put a sticker on each part as it is counted so none is counted twice. Then do the same with a tin and a party hat, and ask where the hat's one vertex is.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which count is this, faces, edges or corners? Second rung, the phase's: has every side of the solid been turned to face you? Third rung: the solid is cut to one face held flat, its edges and corners counted, before the whole solid comes back. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the two tables on the solids page print their columns in different orders, edges before vertices in one and after them in the other, so a number read by its place in a row lands under the wrong word.
wrong.move: swaps the edge and vertex counts, writing eight edges and twelve vertices for a cube.
wrong.screen: the counts are run again one at a time with their headings lit: every edge traced lights amber along its length and the edge count climbs to twelve, then every corner takes a vermilion dot and the vertex count climbs to eight. The child's two numbers stay in the slot beside the headings, nothing marked.

wrong.why: the definition on the solids page says two edges meet at a vertex, and the cone's one edge runs round its rim, nowhere near its tip.
wrong.move: gives the cone no vertex, because a vertex was defined as a point where two edges meet and a cone has only one edge.
wrong.screen: the cone turns on the turntable and its tip is tapped: a vermilion dot drops there and the vertex count takes one, while the edge count, traced round the rim, stays at one. The tip is lit as the cone's corner, where its curved face comes to a point with no edges meeting, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a box on the turntable with its three counters empty
phases.soWhat: A face is a surface, an edge is where two faces meet, and a vertex is a corner. A cube has six faces, twelve edges and eight vertices.

phases.win: the prism shows two matching bases with rectangles between, and the pyramid one square base with four triangles meeting at its tip
phases.does: lights the bases of each solid, counts them, and sets each under prism or pyramid
phases.goal: a prism has two matching bases joined by rectangles, and a pyramid has one base with triangles rising to a point
phases.says: How many bases does it have? What joins them, or where do its sides meet?
phases.check: A pyramid has a base with six sides. How many faces does it have? What shape is each one?
phases.feels: a prism has two matching ends, a pyramid has one base and a point, and the base keeps whatever shape it has
phases.hands: Set out a cube, a tall carton with square ends, a tent-shaped card box and a paper pyramid on a square base. Ask which have two matching ends and which have one base with triangles rising to a point. Then stand a ruler against the tall carton and against one edge of its square end, and ask whether it is a cube.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many bases does the solid have? Second rung, the phase's: what shape is the base, and what joins it to the rest? Third rung: the bench is cut to one solid, lit base first, and each other face is lit in turn before the second solid comes back. The number pad and the word pad stay open.

wrong.why: the solids page says a pyramid's faces are all triangular, beside a table that gives the square pyramid a square base.
wrong.move: says every face of a square pyramid is a triangle, and counts only the four that rise to the tip.
wrong.screen: the base light turns the pyramid over and lights its base green: a square, with four sides and four corners. The face count climbs to five, the four triangles and the square, and the child's four stays in the slot beside it.

wrong.why: the solids page lists a square prism as also known as a cube and never mentions its height, and a cube is a square prism only when its height matches the side of its base.
wrong.move: calls a tall square prism a cube because its two ends are squares.
wrong.screen: the size strip is laid up the prism's side and along one edge of its square end, and the two lengths stand side by side, the height plainly longer. The prism is shrunk down until the two lengths match, and only then do all six faces light as squares. The child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a triangular prism and a square pyramid on the sorting bench with their bases dim
phases.soWhat: A prism has two matching bases joined by rectangles; a pyramid has one base, and its faces other than the base are triangles meeting at a point.

phases.win: the net closes into a cube with every edge met, or shows the two faces that collide and the side left open
phases.does: folds the net up along its edges and watches whether every edge meets
phases.goal: a net is a flat shape that folds along its edges into a solid, and some arrangements of squares do not fold into a cube
phases.says: Fold it up. Does it close, or do two faces land in one place?
phases.check: Draw two different nets of a cube on squared paper. Cut one out and fold it to check.
phases.feels: the count of squares is not enough; where each square hangs decides whether it closes
phases.hands: Give each group a cardboard box to cut along some of its edges until it lies flat in one piece, and compare the flat shapes from different groups. Then give each group six paper squares and ask them to tape together one flat piece that folds back into a cube, and one that does not.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many faces does the solid need? Second rung, the phase's: which squares fold up to make the top and the bottom? Third rung: the net is folded one crease at a time, with the child choosing each next crease. The word pad stays open.

wrong.why: a cross looks like a box opened out flat, and one picture of a net looks like the only one.
wrong.move: thinks a net of a cube must be shaped like a cross, and says a different arrangement of six squares cannot fold into one.
wrong.screen: the child's arrangement, a row of four with one square above the first and one below the last, is laid on the bench and folded up one crease at a time: the row wraps round into four sides and the other two squares fold over as the top and the bottom, closing with every edge met. The cross is folded beside it and closes too, and both cubes stand side by side with the child's answer in the slot.

wrong.why: six faces and six squares match, so the count looks like the whole test.
wrong.move: expects six squares in a straight row to fold into a cube, because there are six squares and a cube has six faces.
wrong.screen: the row is folded up one crease at a time: it wraps round, and the fifth and sixth squares land on the first and second, glowing sky blue where two faces sit in one place, while the top and the bottom of the box stay open. The child's answer stays in the slot, nothing marked.

phases.screen: six squares joined as one flat piece on the net bench
phases.soWhat: A net is a flat shape that folds along its edges into a solid, and one solid can have several nets.
phases.concept: A net folds into a solid

phases.win: the three views settle at one scale, the front and side views standing the same height
phases.does: opens each camera in turn and matches the measurements the views share
phases.goal: a solid looks different from the top, the front and the side, and every view of one solid shares its measurements
phases.says: Look from the top, then the front, then the side. Which views are the same height?
phases.check: A box is nine centimetres long, three wide and five high. Give its top view, its front view and its side view.
phases.feels: each camera sees one side of the same box, so the views share its measurements
phases.hands: Stand a box on a desk. Ask one child to look from directly above, one from the front and one from the side, and each to sketch what they see. Hold the front and side sketches side by side, and ask whether they should be the same height.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which camera is looking? Second rung, the phase's: which two measurements does that camera see? Third rung: the solid is cut to a cube, whose three views are three equal squares, before the box comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the solids page draws a box's side view taller than its front view, and a narrow view drawn tall looks right.
wrong.move: draws the side view of a box taller than its front view.
wrong.screen: the size strip holds the box's height, and the front and side views are both drawn against it at one scale, with level guide lines running from the top of one to the top of the other. The child's taller side view stands beside them, its top above the guide line, and both are kept.

wrong.why: the rectangle is the shape the cylinder shows from the front, which is how it is usually seen.
wrong.move: gives an upright cylinder a rectangle as its top view.
wrong.screen: the top camera is opened over the upright cylinder, and its view is drawn as a plain circle with no dot, the front camera's rectangle drawn beside it. The view window labels each drawing with the camera that saw it, and the child's rectangle stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a box on the turntable with three cameras round it and the view window empty
phases.soWhat: A solid looks different from the top, the front and the side, and the views share its measurements: a box's front and side views are the same height.

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment the last crease of a good net is folded. The squares have been rising one at a time along their edges, and as the last one swings up to close the top, every edge meets its partner with a soft click, the seams disappear, and the finished cube drops onto the turntable and turns once. Unfold it and the six squares lie flat again exactly where they began. It can be folded and unfolded as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a closed box sits on the turntable with its hidden edges dashed and its three counts at nothing. On the second a triangular prism and a square pyramid stand on the bench under the headings prism and pyramid, with their bases dim. On the third six squares lie on the bench as one flat piece, not yet folded. On the fourth a box stands on the turntable with three small cameras round it, the view window empty and the size strip holding the box's measurements. The running count at the top left holds the faces, the edges and the vertices, the corners, counted so far, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the box's top face, or the prism's end, or the first crease of the net, or the top camera, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what will be counted first. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any solid on the turntable, any net on the bench, and the view window open on either. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on counting faces, edges and vertices, telling prisms from pyramids, which nets fold into a solid, and top, front and side views.
voiceLines: A solid on a turntable. What will you count first, faces, edges or corners?
Spin it round. Count the faces first, then the edges, then the corners.
How many bases does it have? What joins them, or where do its sides meet?
Fold it up. Does it close, or do two faces land in one place?
Look from the top, then the front, then the side. Which views are the same height?
A new solid. Turn it right round before you count anything.
Free play. Any solid, any net, with the three cameras open.
Spin it slowly and count again, one kind of part at a time.
Every part counted under its heading, every base found, every net folded and every view drawn.

observations.why: A box has edges on its far side that a single view cannot show.
observations.soWhat: Count faces, edges and vertices on the whole solid, turning it, and read each count by its heading.
observations.observe: The edge count reached twelve only after the turntable brought the hidden edges round.

observations.why: A pyramid has one base, and only the faces other than the base rise to its point as triangles.
observations.soWhat: A pyramid's faces other than its base are triangles, and its base can be a square or another polygon.
observations.observe: The square pyramid lit one square face and four triangles.

observations.why: A net closes only when every face lands in a different place and every edge meets another.
observations.soWhat: A net is tested by folding: six squares are not enough on their own, and a cube has several nets.
observations.observe: Six squares in a row wrapped round and two faces landed in one place, while other arrangements of six closed into a cube.

observations.why: Both cameras see the same height of the same box.
observations.soWhat: The views of one solid share its measurements, so a side view is never taller than the front view of the same box.
observations.observe: The front and side views of the box stood level against the same guide line.

description: Count a solid's faces, edges and vertices, tell a prism from a pyramid, fold a flat net into a solid, and look at a box from the top, the front and the side.

serves.exercise: finding out about more solids and identifying their faces, vertices and edges
identifying the top view of a cone and of an upright cylinder

source_tool.description: A solid stands on a turntable in the middle of the stage and can be spun to show every side. Tapping a face lights it and adds it to a face count, tracing along a line where two faces meet lights an edge and adds it to an edge count, and tapping a corner drops a dot on a vertex and adds it to a vertex count, with the three counts kept apart at the top left of the canvas. A curved face is lit as curved and a flat one as flat, and a cone's tip takes a dot as its one vertex though no two edges meet there. A sorting bench lights the base of a solid: a prism shows two matching bases with rectangles joining them, and a pyramid shows one base with triangles rising from its sides to meet at a point, the base itself staying whatever shape it is. A net bench lays a flat net of squares, rectangles or triangles on the table and folds it up along its edges; a net that makes a solid closes with every edge met, and one that does not shows two faces landing on the same place and a side left open. A view window sets three small cameras, one above, one in front and one at the side, and draws each view at the same scale, so the front and side views of a box stand the same height.
source_tool.art_direction: Solids on a turntable and nets / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a drawing board with a ruler and a point stamp, a tracing finger and a flag, a walker and a string, square tiles on squared paper, a pair of compasses with a metal point and a pencil arm, a sheet of paper that folds, an upright mirror, solids on a turntable, flat nets that fold up, hinged arms, a clock face and a grid of pictures.

A line is always drawn with an arrowhead at each end, a ray with a dot at its end point and one arrowhead, and a line segment with a dot at each end. No stroke is ever left with a bare end that could be read as either.

A point is drawn as one small dot of one size wherever it appears, named by a capital letter beside it. Within one figure no letter ever names two different things, and a figure never renames a part it has already named.

Every labelled length is one the figure could really have, and every figure is drawn to scale with its labels. A triangle drawn with a square corner carries lengths such as three, four and five, and a stepped shape's sides close up exactly.
A figure on squared paper sits exactly on the grid lines, with every side along a line and every square either wholly inside it or wholly outside it.

A circle drawn to show its parts has its centre marked as a dot and named. Every radius is drawn from that dot to the curve, and a diameter always passes exactly through the dot. A circle that is a view of a solid carries a dot only where the solid has a point, so a cylinder seen from above is a plain circle.
A right angle carries a small square corner mark, and every other angle an arc drawn close to its vertex between the arms.

A line of symmetry and a mirror line are drawn dotted and lie exactly where the fold falls. A fold line being tried is drawn solid and turns dotted only once the fold is kept. Every mirror line stands upright unless the frame says it lies across, and an image sits exactly as far behind the line as the thing in front of it, turned the other way round.
A solid is drawn with its hidden edges dashed. Views of one solid are drawn at one scale, so the front view and the side view of a box are exactly the same height.

Clock hands point exactly at the numbers and the minute hand is the longer. Where the angle between the hands is shown, both angles are shaded and the smaller one is outlined. No clock is set to six o'clock or twelve o'clock.
A grid carries its row numbers down the left edge and its column numbers across the top, and each picture in it appears once.
A shape, a side or a part is told apart by its label first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a line, a point, a square or a part the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The figure being studied, every line, segment, ray, side, outline, circle, angle arm and visible edge of a solid, is deep blue. Every point, end point, corner dot, vertex dot and the centre dot of a circle is vermilion, in every tool without exception, because a chapter that opens on the point cannot afford a frame where a point has to be hunted for. A length being measured, walked, added or named, the tape, the walker's sum, a radius being measured, and every angle arc and square corner mark, is amber. The unit squares that cover an area, the flood inside a closed figure and a face of a solid being counted are green. A line of symmetry or a mirror line is reddish purple and always dotted, so a dotted line always means a true line of symmetry. Sky blue is the second thing set beside the first: a fold being tried, drawn solid until it is kept, a mirror image, the other half of a fold, a chord that is not a diameter, and the larger angle between clock hands. A hidden edge of a solid is grey and dashed, and grey is used for nothing else. Every grid line, ruler tick, bracket, guide line and table rule is near-black chrome. All of that holds in greyscale, because a point is a round dot, a measured length carries its number, a line of symmetry is dotted, a fold being tried is solid and a hidden edge is dashed.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Spin it slowly and count again, one kind of part at a time.
voice.onNext: A new solid. Turn it right round before you count anything.
voice.opening: A solid on a turntable. What will you count first, faces, edges or corners?
voice.onFinish: Every part counted under its heading, every base found, every net folded and every view drawn.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any solid, any net, with the three cameras open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: A net folds into a solid

placement.where: After a cardboard box has been counted and cut along some edges until it lies flat in one piece. The tool is what folds a net back up and shows two faces landing on one place when it will not close, and draws three views of one box at one scale, neither of which a flat page can do.

answer_key.rule: A solid is a three-dimensional object that takes up space. A face is a surface of a solid, flat or curved; an edge is where two faces meet; and a vertex is a corner. A cube and a cuboid each have six faces, twelve edges and eight vertices. A cylinder has two flat faces, one curved face and two edges; a cone has one flat face, one curved face, one edge and one vertex, its tip; a sphere has one curved face. A prism has two matching bases and rectangles for its other faces, and it is named by the shape of its bases. A pyramid has one base, and the faces other than the base are triangles that meet at a point; a square pyramid has a square base. A square prism is a cube only when its height equals the side of its square base. A net is a flat shape that folds along its edges into a solid, and one solid can have several nets. A solid looks different from the top, the front and the side, and views of one solid share its measurements: the front and side views of a box are the same height.
answer_key.wrong: The solid is spun slowly with every counted part left lit, the net is unfolded and folded again one crease at a time, and the views are redrawn beside the solid they came from. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Count the flat faces: top, bottom and four round the sides, which makes six.
Count the edges, where two faces meet: four round the top, four round the bottom and four standing up, which makes twelve.
Count the corners: four at the top and four at the bottom, which makes eight vertices.
items.answer: Six faces, twelve edges and eight vertices
items.question: A die is a cube. How many faces, edges and vertices does it have?
items.checkpoint: A face is a surface, an edge is where two faces meet, and a vertex is a corner.
items.misconception: Counting only the edges that can be seen from one side, and getting nine instead of twelve.

steps: A pyramid has one base, and here the base is a square.
A triangle rises from each of the square's four sides, and the four triangles meet at a point.
So its faces are one square and four triangles, five in all; not all of them are triangles.
items.answer: The other faces are four triangles, so it has five faces: the square base and four triangles
items.question: A roof is shaped like a pyramid with a square base. What shape are its other faces, and how many faces does it have in all?
items.checkpoint: A pyramid has one base, and the faces other than the base are triangles meeting at a point.
items.misconception: Saying every face of a pyramid is a triangle and forgetting its square base.

steps: Fold the row of four round so its end squares meet, making the four side faces of a box.
The square above the first folds over to cover the top of the box.
The square below the last folds under to cover the bottom, so every face is covered once and the net closes into a cube.
items.answer: Yes. The row of four wraps round to make the four side faces, and the other two fold to make the top and the bottom
items.question: Six squares are cut out as one piece: a row of four, with one square above the first and one square below the last. Will it fold into a cube?
items.checkpoint: A net is a flat shape that folds along its edges into a solid.
items.misconception: Thinking a net of a cube must be shaped like a cross, so that any other arrangement cannot fold.

steps: From the top you see its length and width, so the top view is ten centimetres by four.
From the front you see its length and height, ten by six; from the side, its width and height, four by six.
The front and side views are both six centimetres high, because they show the same box's height.
items.answer: The top view is a rectangle ten by four, the front view ten by six, and the side view four by six
items.question: A box is ten centimetres long, four centimetres wide and six centimetres high. What are its top view, front view and side view?
items.checkpoint: Every view of one solid shares its measurements, so the front and side views of a box are the same height.
items.misconception: Drawing the side view taller or shorter than the front view, as though the box changed height.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A tin is a cylinder. Count its faces, edges and vertices.
items.final_answer: Three faces, two flat and one curved; two edges; and no vertices

items.question: A party hat is a cone. Count its faces, edges and vertices.
items.final_answer: Two faces, one curved and one flat; one edge round the rim; and one vertex, its tip, though no two edges meet there

items.question: A solid has two matching square ends joined by four rectangles. Is it a prism or a pyramid, and is it a cube?
items.final_answer: A prism, a square prism. It is a cube only if its height is the same as the side of its square ends

items.question: A pyramid has a base with five sides. How many faces does it have?
items.final_answer: Six: the five-sided base and five triangles, one rising from each side of the base

items.question: Six squares are joined in one straight row. Will they fold into a cube?
items.final_answer: No. The row wraps round and the last two squares land on the first two, leaving the top and the bottom open

items.question: A net is a square with a triangle on each of its four sides. Which solid does it fold into?
items.final_answer: A square pyramid: the square is the base, and the four triangles fold up to meet at a point

items.question: A square pyramid stands on its base. What does it look like from directly above?
items.final_answer: A square, with a line from each corner to a point in the middle, where the tip sits over the centre

items.question: A box is twelve centimetres long, five wide and eight high. Give its front view and its side view, and the measurement they share.
items.final_answer: The front view is twelve by eight and the side view five by eight; they share the height, eight centimetres

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: spins the solid to show every side
light each face, edge or corner tapped and keep the three counts apart
lights the base, or both bases, of a solid
sets a solid under prism or pyramid by its bases and other faces
lays a flat net on the table
folds the net along its edges into a solid, or shows where it fails
draws the solid from the top, the front and the side
holds the measurements every view of one solid shares

teaching_notes: Bring a real box and count it before the tool is opened, faces first, then edges, then corners, touching each one. The table on the page does the counting for six solids, and the find-out task above the nets asks for more, so count a solid the table leaves out, such as a pyramid with a five-sided base. Three printed sentences need care. The page says a pyramid's faces are all triangular while its own table gives a square pyramid a square base: say the faces other than the base are triangles. It says a square prism is also known as a cube, which is true only when its height equals the side of its base: say that condition every time. And it defines a vertex as a point where two edges meet, then gives a cone one edge and one vertex: count the cone's tip as its one vertex and do not claim edges meet there. The two tables on that page print edges and vertices in different orders, so read the column heading and not the position. The three views of a box are printed with the side view taller than the front view, though both show the same height; the view window draws them at one scale.
generation_prompt: Build a solids tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A solid is drawn in a simple three-quarter view on a turntable in the working area, with its hidden edges dashed, and the turntable spins it to show every side. Tapping a face lights it and adds one to a face count, tracing along a line where two faces meet lights that edge and adds one to an edge count, and tapping a corner drops a dot and adds one to a vertex count; the three counts sit apart at the top left of the canvas, and nothing is counted twice. Curved faces light with a curved sheen and flat ones without it, and a cone's tip takes a dot as its one vertex. A sorting bench lights a solid's bases and sets it under prism, with two matching bases joined by rectangles, or pyramid, with one base and triangles rising from its sides to a point. A net bench lays a flat net on the table and folds it along its creases into a solid; a net that cannot close shows two faces landing on the same place and a side left open. A view window with three small cameras draws the solid from above, from the front and from the side, all at one scale beside a size strip, so the front and side views of a box are exactly the same height. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Spin the solid and count its faces. Then count its edges and its corners. Find its bases. Fold the net and see whether it closes. Look at the solid from the top, the front and the side.
